title: Climate change is adding measurable heat-illness pressure to U.S. emergency care
source_unit: Climate Central Climate Matters analysis using CDC heat-related emergency-department visit rates and a peer-reviewed temperature-health attribution model
geography: United States; ten HHS regions covering the 50 states, Puerto Rico, Washington, D.C., and six U.S. territories

climate_attributable_heat_illness_rate.unit: percent of the U.S. heat-related emergency-department visit rate

geographic_pattern.value: all regions experienced an increased heat-illness visit rate attributable to climate change

baseline_context.value: heat illness sends more than 67,000 people to US emergency rooms on average each year

observations.method: Climate Central modeled nonlinear relationships between daily maximum temperature and CDC regional heat-related illness emergency-department visit rates, then compared observed temperatures with counterfactual temperatures without human-caused climate change.
observations.uncertainty: The 27% estimate is modelled attribution of a rate, not a count of visits uniquely caused by climate change; it depends on regional temperature-health specification, counterfactual construction, CDC surveillance, and rounded presentation.
observations.subgroup: People seeking emergency care for heat-related illness across the ten HHS regions during the warm season.
observations.counterinterpretation: The analysis does not show that climate change was the only cause of any visit; baseline heat exposure, occupation, housing, age, health status, adaptation, and access to care also shape observed rates.

region_6_observed_rate.unit: heat-related emergency-department visits per 100,000 visits per day, average in Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas

region_6_counterfactual_rate.unit: heat-related emergency-department visits per 100,000 visits per day under the no-human-caused-climate-change counterfactual

regional_exposure.value: southern and western states experienced the highest heat-related emergency-department visit rates

observations.method: Region-specific temperature-health model with population-weighted daily maximum temperatures and counterfactual temperature comparison.
observations.uncertainty: Regional rates are averages and should not be interpreted as individual risk, total cases, or a direct estimate of climate-attributable hospital spending.
observations.subgroup: Residents and emergency-care systems in southern and western HHS regions, especially Region 6.
observations.counterinterpretation: Regional differences can reflect climate, population, occupational exposure, housing, healthcare-seeking, surveillance, and other social conditions rather than temperature alone.

observed_rate.unit: heat-related emergency-department visits per 100,000 visits per day in Alaska, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington

typical_warm_season_rate.unit: heat-related emergency-department visits per 100,000 visits per day in the region over 2018-2025

counterfactual_rate.unit: heat-related emergency-department visits per 100,000 visits per day under the no-human-caused-climate-change counterfactual

climate_attributable_share.unit: percent of the modeled rate during the event

observations.method: Daily regional temperature-health attribution during the identified heat wave compared with the region's typical warm-season rate and counterfactual temperatures.
observations.uncertainty: The event comparison is a modeled rate estimate and does not establish the exact number of climate-caused visits, deaths, or costs; the counterfactual is not directly observable.
observations.subgroup: Residents of Alaska, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington during the June 2021 heat wave.
observations.counterinterpretation: An extreme event can produce unusually high rates through multiple interacting factors, including infrastructure, public warnings, power, housing, behavior, and healthcare access.

household_burden.value: additional heat-related emergency care can increase financial and practical burdens on patients and insurers

hospital_burden.value: additional heat-related demand can increase pressure on already busy and under-resourced hospitals

response_options.value: heat action plans, education, outreach, surveillance, and improved cooling and treatment protocols are identified as capacity responses

observations.method: Interpretation of attribution results alongside public-health and emergency-care response pathways.
observations.uncertainty: The article does not estimate the cost of additional visits, the effectiveness of any named adaptation, or the distribution of burdens across insurance, income, age, race, disability, or housing groups.
observations.subgroup: Patients, households, insurers, hospitals, emergency responders, public-health offices, and communities facing heat exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Preparedness and cooling interventions may reduce illness and emergency demand; increased climate-attributable risk does not imply an unavoidable increase in harm.

related_sources.claim: Climate Central identifies a peer-reviewed Climatic Change study as the full methodology for the attribution analysis.

boundary: This record adds a climate-to-health-system burden pathway for the United States. It measures modeled attribution of heat-related emergency-department visit rates and response implications; it does not establish individual causality, total climate damages, adaptation effectiveness, or equal exposure across social groups.
